{
    "id": "03-memory/cache-management",
    "title": "Cache Management",
    "category": "03-memory",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Operate a bounded cache with explicit admission, TTL expiry, deterministic LRU eviction, and a measured hit rate so memory stays capped and staleness stays bounded by policy.",
    "body": "Cache Management Category: Memory | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A cache becomes a correctness risk the moment it has no policy: unbounded growth exhausts memory, and stale entries serve wrong answers with no bound. This skill defines an explicit cache contract — capacity, TTL, eviction order, and a measured hit rate — so behavior is predictable and observable. It covers in-process caches; distributed cache coherence is out of scope. When to Use Use when an agent or service keeps derived or fetched values in memory and either the memory footprint or the staleness window must stay bounded. Do not use for long-lived stores of record; use the memory and retrieval skills for durable state. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Maximum number of live entries | | | | Yes | Expiry window applied to every entry | | | | No | Injectable clock value for deterministic tests | | | | No | Callback invoked with each evicted key | Procedure 1. Declare capacity and TTL before the first write; never admit an entry without both bounds set. 2. On write, store the value with its absolute expiry timestamp and move the key to the most-recently-used position. 3. Evict least-recently-used entries whenever the live count exceeds capacity; eviction order must be deterministic. 4. On read, treat an expired entry as a miss, delete it, and count it as a miss; never serve a value past its expiry. 5. Count hits and misses on every ac cess so the hit rate is measured, not assumed. 6. Re-measure the hit rate after any capacity or TTL change; an unmeasured cache is a liability, not an optimization. 7. Expose the live size, the measured hit rate, and the eviction count for monitoring. 8. Fail closed on unbounded configurations: a cache without capacity or TTL is rejected, not silently tolerated. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The stored value, or a miss indicator when absent or expired | | | | Accesses served from the cache within expiry | | | | Accesses not served, including expiry misses | | | | Measured hits divided by total accesses over the window | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unbounded growth | Capacity was never set | Reject cache creation without a capacity bound | | Stale serve | Expiry checked lazily or not at all | Check expiry on every read and delete expired entries | | Eviction thrash | Capacity sits below the working set | Measure the hit rate and resize on evidence | | Silent cache | No hit or miss counters exist | Count every access and expose the measured rate | | Clock coupling | Tests read the wall clock directly | Inject the clock so expiry behavior is deterministic | Security and Authority Boundary Operating a cache grants no authority over the source of truth. Cached values are read-only projections; writes flow to the underlying store through its normal controls. Entries holding sensitive data inherit the source’s retention rules: TTL and eviction must not become a way to keep data past its declared lifetime. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s survey of cache replacement policies (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cachereplacementpolicies). 2. Python’s collections module documentation covering OrderedDict (https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.     "description": "Compress long agent context while preserving active task state, user constraints, tool dependencies, and evidence required for correct continuation.",
    "body": "Context Compaction Description Reduce an agent's active context when it approaches a configured budget while preserving the information required to continue correctly. Compaction must preserve active objectives, constraints, decisions, unresolved work, tool dependencies, authoritative evidence, and user-provided requirements while discarding redundant or safely recoverable history. When to Use - Long-running agent sessions approach context limits. - Tool-heavy workflows accumulate large outputs. - Repeated context windows cause cost or latency pressure. - An agent must continue work after a context boundary without restarting. Inputs / Outputs | Area | Contract | |---|---| | Inputs | Conversation state, active task, completed actions, pending actions, evidence, dependencies, and context budget. | | Outputs | Compact continuation state plus a deterministic record of what was retained, discarded, or made recoverable. | | Invariant | The compacted state must not claim completion for unfinished work. | Procedure 1. Detect context pressure before the hard limit. 2. Identify active objective, constraints, current state, dependencies, evidence, and pending actions. 3. Preserve user requirements and facts needed to verify continuation. 4. Collapse redundant tool output and stale narration. 5. Prevent self-referential summaries from re-expanding the context. 6. Validate the compacted state against the active task before resuming. 7. If critical state cannot be preserved, stop and recover from an authoritative checkpoint instead of guessing. Runnable Example Failure Modes - Repeated compaction with no net reduction. - Loss of active task or user constraints. - Dropped tool dependency causing incorrect continuation. - Summary claims a step is complete when it is only planned. - Full transcript repeatedly re-sent to the compression model, creating unnecessary cost. - Compaction failure silently continues with an over-budget context. Recovery Boundary Compaction is a state-preservation operation, not a license to infer missing facts. Missing critical state must produce BLOCKED or trigger an authoritative recovery mechanism. Evidence Public 2026 agent issues document repeated compaction failures, context bloat, lost checkpoints, and substantial token/cost waste in long-running agent workflows. These are direct demand signals for reliable context-management behavior. Related - short-term-memory.md - working-memory.md - long-term-memory.md - state-machine.md - retry-backoff.md"

    "body": "Retention Policy Category: Memory | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Every stored record is a liability as well as an asset: it ages, it contradicts newer facts, and it answers requests you did not invite. A retention policy decides, per class of memory, how long it is kept, why, and what happens at the boundary. This skill structures that policy — classes, floors, ceilings, deletion mechanics — and keeps the decision explicit instead of the default of keeping everything until something breaks. When to Use Use when an agent persists memory across sessions and operates under privacy obligations, data agreements, or plain hygiene requirements. Classify stored memory by purpose — operational, preference, legal, diagnostic — because retention hangs on purpose, not on storage technology. 2. For each class, state the ceiling (how long it may be kept) and any floor (how long it must be kept), with the obligation cited. 3.
